1.text: *Alif-Lãm-Mĩm.* Three letters, no verb, no sentence, and no meaning that any dictionary will give you. The Qurʾān opens its longest sūrah with something that refuses to be a statement, and the first thing to establish is that this is neither an accident nor damage to the text. It is a deliberate device with a name, and the tradition argued about it for centuries without settling it. **What the letters are called.** Maʿārif gives the term and the reason for it: each of these letters is pronounced separately, without a vowel sound added after it, which is why the technical name is *muqaṭṭaʿāt* — isolated or disconnected letters. Tazkīrul Qurʾān supplies the scale of the thing, and the scale matters, because it tells you this is a pattern and not a curiosity: the *muqaṭṭaʿāt* open twenty-nine chapters, in combinations such as *Alif Lām Mīm*, *Hā Mīm*, *Nūn*, *ʿAyn Sīn* and *Qāf*, and some of them became the names of the sūrahs themselves — *Ṭā Hā*, *Yā Sīn*, *Ṣād*, *Qāf*. So a reader meets this device again and again through the Book, and every time it does the same thing. It stops the reading before the reading has started. **The readings on what they mean.** Tanwīr al-Miqbās preserves the fullest list, transmitting from Ibn ʿAbbās: *Alif stands for Allah, Lām for the Archangel Gabriel, and Mīm for Muḥammad.* Then two further readings follow in the same breath — that the three letters stand for Allah's blessings, His kindness and His dominion; or that each is the opening letter of one of His names, *Allāh*, *al-Laṭīf* and *al-Majīd*. And then the reading that ends the list, and outlasted the others: *it is also said that only Allah knows the meaning of these disjointed letters, while some maintain that it is an oath that He made.* Four explanations in one paragraph, and the last is the one that held. **Why the majority stopped there.** Maʿārif records where the weight of opinion settled, and the reasoning is historical rather than clever. Some commentators held that the isolated letters are the names of the sūrahs they open; others that they are symbols of the Divine Names. But the majority of the Companions, of the Tābiʿīn after them, and of the later authoritative scholars preferred the view that they are symbols or mysteries whose meaning is known to Allah alone, or was entrusted to the Prophet ﷺ as a secret not to be passed on. The argument that decides it is the silence: no explanation of these letters was ever reported from him. Had he been given their meaning to convey, he would have conveyed it. Al-Qurṭubī adopted precisely this position. Al-Jalālayn compresses the entire question into five words — *God knows best what He means by these letters* — which is not an evasion but the conclusion the evidence supports. **What the letters are doing instead.** Because if their meaning is closed, their function is not, and Al-Mukhtaṣar states that function in a single move. The letters have no meaning in themselves, yet they have a purpose, and since there is divine wisdom in everything in the Qurʾān, they *point to the miracle of the Qurʾān, made up of the letters which make up the words we speak.* That is the challenge stripped to its shortest form. Here are three of your letters, unarranged and unexplained. The Book that follows is built from the same stock, and you cannot produce it. The letters are not a puzzle to be solved; they are the raw material laid on the table before the argument begins. Al-Mukhtaṣar adds the structural confirmation: sūrahs that begin with these letters are usually followed by a verse about the Qurʾān itself — which is exactly what verse 2 does. **The sūrah they open.** Ibn Kathīr's entry on this verse is not about the letters at all. It is titled the virtues of Sūrat al-Baqarah, and it collects what the sūrah is worth, which is a strange and fitting thing to find attached to three unexplained letters. Abū Hurayrah reports the Prophet ﷺ saying, *Do not turn your houses into graves. Verily, Shayṭān does not enter the house where Sūrat al-Baqarah is recited* — carried by Aḥmad, Muslim, at-Tirmidhī and an-Nasāʾī, and graded ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ. ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd put it more bluntly: Shayṭān flees from the house where al-Baqarah is heard, and ad-Dārīmī preserves his version in which he flees passing wind. The same source gives the practical form: ten āyāt of al-Baqarah recited in a night keep Shayṭān out of the house — four from the beginning, Āyat al-Kursī, the two after it, and the last three. Saḥl ibn Saʿd reports that everything has a high peak and al-Baqarah is the high peak of the Qurʾān. And at-Tirmidhī records the expedition on which the Prophet ﷺ asked each man what he had memorised, came to the youngest, heard that he knew al-Baqarah, and made him commander over men older than himself. One of the notables objected that he had deliberately avoided learning it, for fear he could not implement it. That objection is the point of the sūrah, and of the three letters in front of it. The Book does not open with a summary of its contents. It opens with a demonstration that you cannot make one, and then asks whether you are going to obey it.
